Summary
Since publishing our CPU TAM model in May, we sense investors have extrapolated 
strong near-term demand into more aggressive C2030 TAM outcomes (in some cases 
we have heard ~$300B). We have pushed back against these narratives, instead steering 
such bullish outcomes to a long thesis on MU because we believe DRAM will remain too 
constrained to enable a TAM that large by 2030. All of that said, we do see accelerating 
traction in standalone CPU racks with the architectural split we outlined playing out: 1) 
latency-sensitive head nodes favoring ARM (NVDA Grace/Vera (which we think is

gaining traction due to combination of low latency+multithreading with NVDA offering 
memory as part of the system), Axion, Graviton), and 2) standalone agentic AI racks 
being more core and throughput-driven — an area where we think AMD has a distinct 
advantage. We think INTC retains optionality with x86, but mid-term upside hinges on 
improving its high core-count/performance roadmap. While ARM’s Gen1 CPU is better 
suited for head nodes today, its roadmap (200–500 cores) could become more 
competitive in standalone use cases over time. Net, we raise estimates for AMD and 
ARM as key beneficiaries of standalone CPU and head node deployments, and move PTs

Increasing AMD estimates on higher share expectations in standalone segment
We are incrementally more constructive on AMD as standalone CPU racks gain traction, 
given its advantage in core count, multithreading, and x86's historically strong software 
ecosystem for traditional software workloads that are now increasingly part of the 
agentic AI workloads. We now assume x86/ARM split for standalone segment of the 
market at 60%/40% x86 vs ARM and think AMD is in position to capture an outsized 
share of the incremental demand in light of INTC's roadmap and supply challenges.

text:
INTC's recent launch of 288 e-core Clearwater Forest CPU is roughly equivalent in 
performance (we think) to the low-end (~165 cores) of AMD’s p-core Venice platform 
(which scales all the way to 256 cores). While INTC retains optionality from internal 
manufacturing, mid-term upside depends on improving its high core-count roadmap 
and we expect share to continue to significantly tilt to AMD. We are increasing AMD's 
CPU Server revenues for C26E/C27E/C28E from $16B/$21B/$27B to $16B/$23B/$29B 
and reaching $50B in C2030E (vs prior $41B).  We take our PT to $670 based on an 
unchanged 35x multiple.

We maintain the view that ARM architectures will represent ~70% share of a ~20MM 
unit TAM for head-nodes by C2030 – the real investor debate, in our view, is revenue 
potential for ARM’s standalone CPU (AGI). Following a series of expert calls and industry 
discussions, we emerge slightly more optimistic about its standalone prospects and are 
raising our estimates for ARM’s internal CPU (AGI) slightly from ~$13B to ~$14B in 
C2030. ARM’s core competency lies in latency and efficiency – which aligns well with 
hyperscaler needs – however, current limitations in core count/throughput will limit the
